cards.title: Design a vacation-proof scoreboard with 5–7 near-term results categories
cards.summary: Build a shared, simple, specifically actionable scoreboard of result categories that removes subjective interpretation of success, and review it monthly.
cards.use_when: When setting or refreshing a store's team-level KPI dashboard so individual departments (merch, marketing, CX, ops) cannot pick self-serving metrics.

cards.title: Make every department jointly responsible for revenue and retention
cards.summary: Replace departmental ownership silos with shared accountability so the whole leadership group owns acquisition, retention, merchandising and operations results.
cards.use_when: When store leaders say 'that's marketing's job' or 'that's fulfillment's problem' and no one intervenes cross-functionally to hit a quarter's goals.

cards.title: Define politics behaviorally and stop it with a shared definition
cards.summary: Give the team a crisp definition of politics — choosing words and actions based on how you want others to react rather than what you really think — so lobbying and posturing become recognizable and correctable.
cards.use_when: When store meetings turn into departments lobbying for headcount, budget or shelf space, or when people avoid touching issues outside their own area.

cards.title: Make conflict about ideas, not harmony, and run it inside meetings
cards.summary: Position productive ideological conflict in meetings as the engine of commitment, and treat false harmony and passive sarcasm as the real costs.
cards.use_when: When a store's planning meetings avoid hard trade-offs (assortment cuts, discounting, outsourcing a process) and the same unresolved issue recurs every week.

cards.title: Get buy-in by airing opinions, then disagree and commit
cards.summary: Secure real commitment to a store decision by letting everyone be heard — not by seeking consensus — and by adopting a disagree-and-commit norm.
cards.use_when: When a merchandising, pricing or channel decision is announced and the team quietly under-executes because they never weighed in.

cards.title: Coach strengths and weaknesses around impact, not generic modesty
cards.summary: Run a low-risk vulnerability exercise where each person names their biggest strength and weakness in terms of impact on the business's success or failure.
cards.use_when: When building trust in a new store leadership team, or when an offsite needs a concrete bonding exercise that feeds actual role decisions.

cards.title: Set one overarching goal so individual ego has nowhere to hide
cards.summary: Choose a single near-term overarching goal that channels collective ego toward a shared score, and resolve conflicting department goals in the open.
cards.use_when: When a store's leaders each champion a different priority (market share vs. product quality vs. cost containment) and the portfolio of initiatives dilutes focus.

cards.title: Hold peers accountable even when it's uncomfortable
cards.summary: Introduce peer-to-peer accountability for standards and behavior, recognizing that it is harder between equals than with direct reports and depends on prior buy-in.
cards.use_when: When a store leader tolerates a peer's low standard (late launches, unanswered messages, missed handoffs) to avoid an awkward conversation.

cards.title: Replace quarterly-only oversight with weekly metric reviews
cards.summary: Shift from outsourcing each area's numbers to one owner and reviewing only quarterly, to weekly metric ownership and monthly review windows with mid-period resource shifts.
cards.use_when: When a store only sees performance in income-statement or quarterly terms and can't change course inside the period.

cards.title: Let harsh feedback land before countering
cards.summary: When the team pushes back on a difficult message, absorb the objections, offer a partial genuine apology, then restate the substantive point without backing down.
cards.use_when: When a store leader delivers a hard diagnosis about team performance or culture and gets a defensive pile-on instead of engagement.

cards.title: Read honest resistance as the signal you've been waiting for
cards.summary: Interpret a team's blunt pushback on a change process as engagement and a prerequisite for real change, rather than as failure of the effort.
cards.use_when: When rolling out a new process for a store team (planning cadence, performance reviews, reorg) and you meet open resistance rather than polite compliance.

cards.title: Choose one overarching goal and translate it into a measurable target
cards.summary: Run a forced-choice goal-setting debate that narrows many candidate goals to a single overarching one, then convert it into a specific number with a deadline.
cards.use_when: Setting the store's quarterly or annual priority — deciding whether to optimize for revenue, market share, new customers, repeat customers, or margin.

cards.title: Depth beats breadth for new stores: pick one critical goal
cards.summary: A team can hold one overarching goal at a time; multiple simultaneous priorities dilute focus and stall execution.
cards.use_when: Deciding what the next 90 days of store work is actually for — product range expansion, ad spend, SEO, retention — before allocating budget or headcount.

cards.title: Beliefs and confidences surface constantly — plan for the relapse
cards.summary: After an intense planning or strategy session, expect visible enthusiasm on the day and a rapid return to old behavior within days; plan a follow-up session before the first one ends.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a strategy offsite, brand workshop or planning day for an ecommerce team and deciding whether one session is enough.

cards.title: Diagnose whether each leader's 'first team' is their department or the company
cards.summary: Ask each departmental leader directly who they confide in and prioritize, because loyalties to a department over the company produce gatekeeping and information leaks.
cards.use_when: Investigating why store functions (merchandising, marketing, fulfillment, paid media) undermine each other, withhold information, or refuse to back company priorities over their own team's comfort.

cards.title: Make the team's shared goal the actual agenda of every staff meeting
cards.summary: A recurring meeting should be dominated by working the shared critical number, not by status updates or touchy-feely exercises.
cards.use_when: Engineering a weekly or fortnightly ecommerce ops meeting that currently produces no decisions and no progress on the store's most important number.

cards.title: Define trust as willingness to be pushed, not as assuming alignment
cards.summary: Accountability between colleagues is not distrust; trust is knowing the push comes from caring about the outcome.
cards.use_when: Fixing a store team that avoids challenging each other about slip, quality, or stalled work — e.g. late product photography, unvalidated ad spend, unshipped collections.

cards.title: Handle destructive behavior inside the meeting and ask the offender to choose the venue
cards.summary: A leader who allows public attacks and disengagement to pass effectively endorses them; ask the offender whether to resolve the issue publicly or privately, then follow through.
cards.use_when: A store meeting breaks down — someone insults an absent colleague, mocks another function, or walks out mid-agenda — and the decision is whether to correct it now or later.

cards.title: Confirm role fit with an assignment change before adding headcount
cards.summary: When someone is visibly underutilized and pushing projects out of personal need, test whether a change of scope — not a new acquisition or hire — resolves it.
cards.use_when: A senior team member or key contractor in the store is agitating for a big new initiative, an acquisition, a second brand or a large hire mostly because they are bored.

cards.title: Run a Five Dysfunctions Team Diagnostic
cards.summary: Score your leadership team against the five dysfunctions with a 15-statement questionnaire to find which layer is broken before you fix anything else.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why your ecommerce leadership team (merchandising, growth, ops, supply chain) makes slow or reversed decisions before choosing an intervention like restructuring or new hires.

cards.title: Model the Five Dysfunctions as a Chain, Not Five Projects
cards.summary: Trust, conflict, commitment, accountability and results are a sequential stack — breaking one link undermines the whole team, so diagnose in order rather than fixing symptoms independently.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest management effort when your ecommerce team shows several problems at once (missed launch dates, silent meetings, finger-pointing between merchandising and fulfillment).

cards.title: Behavioral Signs That Distinguish Trusting From Distrusting Teams
cards.summary: Compare your team's observable behaviors against the source's lists of trust symptoms to decide whether the problem is a trust deficit or something else.
cards.use_when: Assessing your ecommerce leadership or cross-functional team (e.g. growth, merchandising and supply chain) after a pattern of stalled decisions or unusual turnover.

cards.title: Define Trust as Vulnerability, Not Reliability
cards.summary: Team trust means peers are confident each other's intentions are good enough to be open about weaknesses and mistakes — predictability alone is not enough.
cards.use_when: Evaluating why your ecommerce team avoids surfacing bad news about a failing SKU, a vendor delay, or a campaign that underperformed, even when individuals reliably deliver their assigned work.

cards.title: Personal Histories Exercise for Faster Team Trust
cards.summary: A sub-hour, low-risk exercise where team members share non-sensitive biographical facts to build empathy and prevent unfair behavioral attributions.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a newly formed ecommerce leadership team, integrating a new head of merchandising or supply chain, or restarting a burned-out cross-functional group after a bad quarter.

cards.title: Team Effectiveness Exercise: One Contribution, One Needed Improvement
cards.summary: Each member names the single most important contribution a peer makes and the one thing that peer must improve or stop, reported one person at a time starting with the leader.
cards.use_when: When a team is functional enough to handle direct feedback but still has unspoken performance or behavior problems — for example, a merchandising lead whose dismissiveness is quietly degrading planning meetings.

cards.title: Use Personality Profiles to Reduce Team Friction
cards.summary: Behavioral preference profiles such as the MBTI give nonjudgmental descriptions of how people think, speak and act, making peer friction easier to interpret and manage.
cards.use_when: When recurring clashes between, say, a data-driven growth lead and an intuitive brand/creative lead are being read as personal conflict instead of stylistic difference.

cards.title: Keep 360-Degree Feedback Out of Compensation
cards.summary: A 360-degree program works only if it is a pure development tool, divorced entirely from pay and formal performance evaluation.
cards.use_when: Rolling out peer feedback across ecommerce functions (merchandising, marketing, ops) and deciding whether it will feed into reviews or salary decisions.

cards.title: Vulnerability Must Start With the Leader — And Cannot Be Staged
cards.summary: The leader must go first in exposing weakness, create an environment that does not punish it, and never fake it for effect.
cards.use_when: When you, as founder or ecommerce lead, want the team to surface bad news about a channel, a vendor, or an assortment bet earlier — but the team still filters what they tell you.

cards.title: Distinguish Productive Ideological Conflict From Personal Attack
cards.summary: Healthy conflict is confined to concepts and ideas and may look passionate or emotional from outside, while personality-focused attacks are destructive and should be ruled out.
cards.use_when: Setting norms for how your ecommerce team debates pricing changes, discount depth, channel budget or a new bundle — before the next planning meeting.

cards.title: Assign a Miner of Conflict to Surface Buried Disagreements
cards.summary: Designate someone in each meeting to extract buried disagreements and force the team to work through them, staying in the discussion until resolution.
cards.use_when: Running an ecommerce planning or S&OP-style meeting where unresolved issues (inventory commitments, promo calendar, channel budget) keep resurfacing instead of being settled.

cards.title: Use 'Real-Time Permission' to Keep Difficult Debates Going
cards.summary: When people start retreating from heated debate, interrupt to tell them the discomfort is appropriate and to keep going — then confirm afterward that the conflict was healthy.
cards.use_when: Facilitating a contentious ecommerce decision — cutting a channel, changing a returns policy, repricing a hero SKU — and watching participants soften their position to reduce tension.

cards.title: Use the Thomas-Kilmann Instrument for Conflict Style Awareness
cards.summary: The TKI helps team members see their default approach to conflict so they can choose tactics deliberately rather than reflexively.
cards.use_when: When the same ecommerce peers repeatedly collide in the same way (e.g. one always yields on assortment calls, another always competes and forces a winner) and you want to change the pattern.

cards.title: Separate Conflict About Issues From Your Team's Job
cards.summary: Leaders arguing about issues in a meeting is the work, not a symptom — resolving it there prevents pushing unsolvable problems down to their teams.
cards.use_when: A leadership meeting over the sales budget, headcount or channel investment turns tense and someone argues the team has regressed.

cards.title: Prepare the Team for the Dip After Early Progress
cards.summary: Warn the team explicitly that progress will be invisible in results for a while, and that groups often slide backward, so early behavioral wins are not mistaken for a finished job.
cards.use_when: Right after an offsite or process reset, before the next quarter's numbers land — so the ecommerce team does not revert when channel performance and morale still look flat.

cards.title: Address Individual Behavior Problems Directly, With Specific Evidence
cards.summary: When a leader's behavior is damaging the team, name it plainly and concretely, tolerate the emotional response, and hold the behavioral requirement firm.
cards.use_when: Handling a genuinely damaging team member — a merchandising or marketing lead whose dismissiveness is undermining peers — and deciding whether to attempt a turnaround or an exit.

cards.title: Address destructive behavior even when a store specialist delivers strong results
cards.summary: Tolerating a high producer's destructive behavior makes the manager — not the individual — responsible for the team's performance collapse.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to protect a top-performing ecommerce buyer, media buyer or engineer whose poor collaboration is driving colleagues out.

cards.title: Let Departures Be Mourned, Then Reframe the Decision
cards.summary: Even the removal of a difficult team member triggers mourning and self-doubt among peers; address it openly rather than letting it dampen the work.
cards.use_when: After terminating or losing a senior ecommerce leader, and noticing the leadership team's energy and meeting quality drop in the following days.

cards.title: Sequence the Communication After a Senior Departure
cards.summary: Announce a departure plainly to the team, hold legal detail back, and handle employee and press messaging with a single consistent line.
cards.use_when: Managing the internal and external messaging after a senior ecommerce leader leaves — before employees hear it from someone else or a trade publication calls.

cards.title: Run an Internal vs External Succession Debate, Then Decide
cards.summary: Have the team debate the replacement decision openly, then make the call yourself and state the criteria the hire must demonstrate.
cards.use_when: Filling a senior ecommerce vacancy — head of marketing, merchandising or supply chain — when there is pressure to promote internally from the existing team.

cards.title: Onboard a New Executive Through the Team, Not a Manual
cards.summary: Have existing team members each teach one dysfunction to the newcomer, then review working style and launch into real debates immediately.
cards.use_when: Integrating a new senior hire — a marketing, supply chain or growth leader — into an established leadership team.

cards.title: Review leadership span when store coordination becomes unwieldy
cards.summary: Reconsider decision ownership and reporting relationships when an expanding store leadership group slows execution.
cards.use_when: Your ecommerce company has grown past roughly a couple of hundred employees and the leadership meeting has become too large for fluid, substantive discussion.

cards.title: Use TKI to Understand Conflict Styles on the Team
cards.summary: The Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument helps team members see their natural conflict inclinations so they can make more strategic choices about which approach fits each situation.
cards.use_when: Team friction is slowing a merchandising, pricing, or vendor-negotiation decision, and the operator wants to help the team choose an appropriate conflict approach rather than defaulting to their habits.

cards.title: Leader Restraint During Team Conflict
cards.summary: Leaders who jump in to protect members from disagreement deprive the team of the chance to develop conflict-management skills; restraint is the harder and more effective choice.
cards.use_when: An operator is tempted to step into a merchandising or marketing disagreement between team members because they fear the conflict is becoming unproductive.

cards.title: Commitment Comes from Clarity and Buy-In, Not Consensus
cards.summary: Great teams make clear, timely decisions and achieve full buy-in even when members disagree, understanding that consensus is not required for support.
cards.use_when: An operator is trying to get the whole team behind a product launch, pricing change, or campaign decision and is tempted to delay until everyone agrees.

cards.title: Use Cascading Messaging to Align the Team and the Organization
cards.summary: A short end-of-meeting exercise where the team reviews key decisions and agrees what to communicate prevents small executive misalignments from becoming major discrepancies downstream.
cards.use_when: A weekly or quarterly ecommerce team meeting is ending and decisions need to be communicated to store staff, vendors, or cross-functional partners.

cards.title: Set and Honor Decision Deadlines
cards.summary: Clear deadlines for decisions — including intermediate milestones — are a primary tool for overcoming commitment dysfunction and preventing costly ambiguity.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team is stalling on a pricing decision, assortment change, or campaign launch and keeps revisiting the same debate.

cards.title: Worst-Case Scenario and Contingency Planning to Reduce Fear of Deciding
cards.summary: Briefly clarifying the worst-case outcome of a decision lets a hesitant team see that the costs of being wrong are survivable and smaller than imagined.
cards.use_when: A team is frozen on a high-stakes decision such as entering a new channel, launching a major product, or committing to a large marketing spend.

cards.title: Low-Risk Exposure Therapy for Commitment-Phobic Teams
cards.summary: Deliberately making decisions in low-risk situations with substantial discussion but little analysis builds the team's confidence and reveals it overvalues lengthy study.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team habitually delays decisions until exhaustive analysis is done, and the operator wants to build the muscle of deciding without perfect information.

cards.title: Leader's Role in Building Commitment
cards.summary: The leader must be comfortable being wrong, constantly push for closure, and avoid placing too high a premium on certainty or consensus.
cards.use_when: An operator leads a team that keeps deferring decisions and needs to set the tone that bold decisions with course-correction are acceptable.

cards.title: Peer Accountability Over Bureaucratic Performance Management
cards.summary: The most effective way to maintain high standards is peer pressure — team members calling each other on behavior — which reduces the need for excessive bureaucracy.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team has performance or behavior problems and the operator is considering adding new policies or formal corrective processes.

cards.title: Publication of Goals and Standards Enables Accountability
cards.summary: Publicly clarifying what the team must achieve, who delivers what, and how everyone must behave makes accountability concrete and removes ambiguity.
cards.use_when: An operator wants to make it easier for team members to hold each other accountable on a new initiative or across a cross-functional project.

cards.title: Simple and Regular Progress Reviews for Accountability
cards.summary: A little structure goes a long way: regular verbal or written communication about how teammates are doing against stated objectives prevents avoidance of accountability.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team is not giving each other feedback on performance, and the operator wants a lightweight review rhythm that surfaces problems early.

cards.title: Team Rewards to Build a Culture of Accountability
cards.summary: Shifting rewards from individual performance to team achievement creates a culture where peers are unlikely to stand by quietly while someone fails to pull their weight.
cards.use_when: An operator is designing incentives for a store team — merchandising, marketing, fulfillment — and wants execution to depend on collective results rather than individual metrics alone.

cards.title: Leader's Role: Avoid the Accountability Vacuum
cards.summary: Strong leaders can accidentally become the only source of discipline; the goal is to let the team be the primary accountability mechanism, with the leader as rare final arbiter.
cards.use_when: An operator finds that team members only raise problems to them, not to each other, and wants to shift accountability to the team.

cards.title: Focus on Results, Not Team or Individual Status
cards.summary: The ultimate dysfunction is caring about something other than collective goals; teams get distracted by team status (just belonging) or individual status (personal advancement).
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team seems comfortable but is not hitting growth or profitability goals, or members are optimizing for their own function rather than the store's collective outcome.

cards.title: Public Declaration of Results
cards.summary: Teams that publicly commit to specific results are more likely to work with a passionate, even desperate desire to achieve them; 'we'll do our best' is a subtle preparation for failure.
cards.use_when: An operator wants a team or the whole store organization to raise its ambition and accountability around a growth or turnaround target.

cards.title: Results-Based Rewards
cards.summary: Tying rewards, especially compensation, to the achievement of specific outcomes keeps attention on results, though relying on this alone assumes financial motivation is the sole driver.
cards.use_when: An operator is setting bonuses or recognition for a team and wants to avoid rewarding effort in the absence of results.

cards.title: Leader Sets the Tone for Results Focus
cards.summary: If team members sense the leader values anything other than results, they take that as permission to do the same; leaders must be selfless and objective in rewards and recognition.
cards.use_when: An operator wants to build or repair a results-focused culture and is examining whether their own behavior is reinforcing or undermining it.

cards.title: Kathryn's Meeting Cadence: How Much Time a Strong Team Spends Together
cards.summary: Kathryn's model shows a management team spending roughly eight days per quarter together — fewer than three days per month — which saves time by eliminating confusion and minimizing redundant effort.
cards.use_when: An operator is deciding how much meeting time the management team needs and is weighing 'real work' against structured team time.

cards.title: Choose FBA or FBM before setting up a seller account
cards.summary: FBA hands pick/pack/ship to Amazon for per-order fees; FBM means you ship yourself, and the source's preference is FBA for a semi-passive operation.
cards.use_when: Deciding your fulfilment model before registering an Amazon seller account or sourcing inventory.

cards.title: Pick an Amazon business model: arbitrage, wholesale or private label
cards.summary: The three Amazon selling routes differ in capital, competition and learning curve; the source suggests starting with arbitrage/wholesale before private label.
cards.use_when: Choosing which Amazon selling model to launch next quarter and how much capital to allocate.

cards.title: Register a UK Amazon Professional seller account and pass verification
cards.summary: Practical setup sequence for a UK seller account, including the live video verification call and proof documents you must have ready.
cards.use_when: Opening a new Amazon seller account in the UK and preparing for identity verification.

cards.title: Set up a seller account you can actually trade from
cards.summary: The account needs verified identity, a linked bank account and the correct plan before any listing work begins.
cards.use_when: Preparing a newly approved seller account before adding your first ASIN.

cards.title: Analyse a resale ASIN with four pass/fail checks
cards.summary: Screen any wholesale or arbitrage product against BSR, seller count, Amazon-as-competitor and ROI before buying.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to buy a specific branded ASIN for Amazon wholesale or arbitrage.

cards.title: Calculate Amazon contribution, inventory ROI and applicable fee taxes
cards.summary: Include the complete per-unit cost stack and the seller's actual tax treatment when screening inventory.
cards.use_when: Judging whether a UK ASIN clears your profit threshold before committing to buy stock.

cards.title: Run a 10–50 unit test order before committing to wholesale stock
cards.summary: The first order for any new wholesale product should be small so you can validate sell-through, competition and eligibility before scaling.
cards.use_when: Placing your first purchase order for a newly validated wholesale ASIN.

cards.title: Add an existing ASIN to your inventory instead of creating a listing
cards.summary: Match existing listings by ASIN, sell at the lowest FBA price and select Amazon's barcode to avoid commingled stock.
cards.use_when: Listing a validated wholesale or arbitrage product you are ready to sell on Amazon.

cards.title: Create an FBA shipping plan and respect box size and weight limits
cards.summary: Create an inbound plan from actual units, packaging and current marketplace requirements.
cards.use_when: Building a shipment plan to send stock from your premises into an Amazon fulfilment centre.

cards.title: Print SKU and box labels and schedule a UPS collection
cards.summary: After confirming the shipment you still must print labels, get the tracking ID and book a UPS pickup — receiving tracking alone is not the end of the process.
cards.use_when: Finalising an FBA shipment after confirming charges in Seller Central.

cards.title: Anti-portfolio: products to avoid when selecting an FBA item
cards.summary: Reject cheap, seasonal, trendy, gated, and patented products before spending on inventory to avoid dead stock and price wars.
cards.use_when: Screening candidate products for a new Amazon FBA listing before committing capital to inventory.

cards.title: Four viability criteria for a target FBA product
cards.summary: Target premium-priced products with 30%+ net margin, problem-solving function, and low brand dominance.
cards.use_when: Building the shortlist of products worth deeper keyword and competitor analysis for an Amazon launch.

cards.title: Keyword variability test: count the ways a product is searched
cards.summary: Prefer products describable by many distinct long-tail keywords so you can rank on multiple first-page terms instead of one contested head term.
cards.use_when: Deciding between two candidate products, or judging whether a niche offers cheap organic entry for a new Amazon listing.

cards.title: Price-disparity check on Page 1 search results
cards.summary: Discard products whose Page 1 prices are tightly clustered; prefer wide spreads so you do not compete solely on price.
cards.use_when: Validating a candidate product's pricing power before sourcing inventory for an Amazon listing.

cards.title: Helium 10 Black Box filter stack for finding weak competitors
cards.summary: A strict numeric filter set to isolate high-revenue, low-sophistication, ungated FBA competitors.
cards.use_when: Running a first-pass product scan in Helium 10 Black Box (Products tab) to generate raw candidates for an Amazon FBA launch.

cards.title: Review mining: turn 4.1–4.3 star sellers into a product spec
cards.summary: Sort results by lowest rating, find mediocre-but-selling products, and read 1-star reviews to extract the exact improvements to brief a supplier.
cards.use_when: Turning a shortlisted FBA candidate into a manufacturing brief before contacting suppliers.

cards.title: Giftability and demand screening before committing to a product
cards.summary: Favor products that work as gifts for multiple holidays or for self-purchase, because Q4 and seasonal events add demand spikes.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing among otherwise-viable FBA candidates, especially when planning a launch calendar around Q4 or holidays.

cards.title: Budget-matched revenue ceiling for new FBA sellers
cards.summary: Choose products whose monthly revenue matches the inventory and ad budget you can actually fund, not the biggest revenue number you can find.
cards.use_when: Setting the Monthly Revenue filter or choosing between candidates when planning first inventory buy-in for an FBA launch.

cards.title: Validate a Product Idea Through a Free Channel Before Amazon FBA
cards.summary: Use a cheap prototype and eBay to confirm demand before committing money to an Amazon FBA launch.
cards.use_when: Product selection: you have a product idea and want to test demand before spending on production runs, branding or Amazon inventory.

cards.title: FBA Economics: Trace Revenue to Profit Line by Line
cards.summary: Break an FBA product's revenue into product cost, Amazon fees, advertising, logistics and true profit to judge viability.
cards.use_when: Product selection and pricing: deciding whether a candidate product can carry all FBA costs and still leave a profit, or diagnosing why a live product isn't profitable.

cards.title: Follow the Five-Step FBA Launch Sequence
cards.summary: Structure an Amazon FBA business as product research, manufacturing, branding, listing, then launch.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing your Amazon FBA roadmap — deciding what the next concrete task is at each stage.
